comparator.name: European Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 curriculum comprises 60 EC in each year. The example follows the first-listed options in each restricted choice group and the first-listed thesis route. The fifth semester contains 24 EC of electives. The final semester includes two courses and either a 17 EC thesis with a 4 EC methods course or a 21 EC Final Project.

core: European history and the making of political orders and identities: Imagining Europe (the development of European identities) and Ruling Europe (the making and unmaking of political orders after the French Revolution), with history named by the programme as one of its integrated disciplines and a Central and Eastern Europe course in year 3.

European integration, EU institutions and political science: Constructing Europe (institutions, theories and challenges in EU politics), the year-level focal point of European unity, the interaction of European institutions and national governments, and policy analysis of European problems.

EU law and legal interpretation: Ordering Europe (the new autonomous legal order) and EU Law II, with law named as one of the integrated disciplines and legislation interpretation taught as a skills training.

Europe in the wider world and international relations: Globalizing World (contemporary issues and actors in international relations), the third year-level focal point of Europe's place in the wider world, the question what role a united Europe can play in international politics, and European Diplomacy in the 21st Century.

Economics of European integration: Governing the European Economy (between market and state) and International Economics and European Integration, with economics named as one of the integrated disciplines.

Political ideas, philosophy and sociology of European societies: philosophy and sociology named as integrated disciplines, with year-3 options on social change, identity and collective action and on controversies in contemporary political philosophy (freedom, justice and inequality).

Democracy, rule of law and accountability: democratic resilience named by the programme as a central challenge, Challenges in Contemporary Democracies as a year-2 option, and the question whether the elected European Parliament can exercise democratic control over Europe's governance.

Research methods, research skills and independent research: the skills trajectory of academic research and writing, working with research problems, working with sources, the Academic Workshops, introductory qualitative and quantitative methods and a choice of interviewing, document analysis or survey research, culminating in the Bachelor Thesis or Final Project.
Professional skills in negotiation, presentation and language: the Negotiation Skills module, skills trainings in presentation skills and international negotiations, and the second-language skill.
adjacent: European climate policy: the programme names climate policy as a headline challenge and climate change as a crisis that cannot be understood from an economic, political or legal perspective alone, with Authority, Expertise and Environmental Change as a year-2 course option.

Europe's diversity, borders, belonging and migration: European diversity is the first year-level focal point, students examine who and what is included in Europe and how borders are defined, and migration is named as a major contemporary challenge.
questions: How do European institutions and national governments interact, and does the elected European Parliament have enough power to exercise democratic control over Europe's governance?
What role can a united Europe play in international politics?
How can Europe respond to crises such as climate change that cannot be understood from an economic, political or legal perspective alone?

trace: examines law from legal, socio-scientific and normative perspectives, covering legal traditions and the fields of constitutional, administrative, international and private law, with case law and a moot court; it is the legal foundation and formal prerequisite for European Union law, comparative constitutional law and public international law, and makes a specific complementary contribution to the legal-analysis strand rather than teaching EU law itself

introduces the EU legal order through its institutional framework, citizenship and the internal market, using problem-based exercises; it directly implements the EU-law component of the target, although as a single foundations course rather than the two-course sequence of Ordering Europe and EU Law II

explores constitutional law and state organisation comparatively, including separation of powers, judicial review, federalism, fundamental rights and constitutional backsliding; it directly addresses the rule-of-law and democratic-backsliding interests and trains legal interpretation, but it is not EU law

introduces public international law through its sources, treaties, the UN, the use of force and refugee law; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the legal dimension of Europe's external relations, and it is not a course on the external relations of the EU

studies human rights as positive law, through treaties, monitoring mechanisms and case law, and as history and philosophy; it makes a specific contribution to fundamental rights and legal interpretation within the rule-of-law strand, although it is not specific to Europe

introduces EU politics through its actors, institutions and decision-making rules, responses to crises and approaches to studying policy-making; it directly implements the EU institutions and integration component of the target

provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies, including democratic backsliding, the decline of political parties, populism and non-majoritarian institutions; it directly implements political-science comparison and the democratic-accountability interest, without a European focus

teaches the main schools of international relations theory and applies them to contemporary global issues, including a UN Security Council negotiation simulation; it directly implements the international relations component of the target, with a global rather than European focus

examines authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights and pluralism through classical and contemporary political-philosophy texts; it directly addresses the philosophy and political-ideas strand of the target

gives a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present, covering industrialisation, popular sovereignty, national self-determination, revolutions, the world wars and the fall of communism; it directly covers the period and the political-order themes of Ruling Europe, although it is not Europe-specific and does not offer the European-identity focus of Imagining Europe

examines the rise and fall of empires, theories of empire and power politics through major historical examples; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the history of political orders and of the external power of European states, without being a course on Europe

guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from research questions to critical engagement with sources, using historical and archival research methods, and ends in a substantial research paper; it directly implements the source-based research training of the target's skills trajectory

introduces microeconomics and macroeconomics, including supply and demand, game theory, market structure, aggregate output, unemployment and inflation; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the economic foundation for the economics-of-integration strand, without European content
Studies business cycles, growth and monetary and fiscal policy in open economies, supplying macroeconomic tools for studying European integration.

investigates the role of government in the economy, including market failure, public goods, taxation, public spending, redistribution and political economy; it directly addresses the market-versus-state theme of Governing the European Economy and supports policy analysis, without EU-specific content

teaches the logic and design of research, sampling, surveys, experiments and descriptive and inferential statistics; it directly implements the quantitative-methods and survey-research training of the target's skills trajectory

introduces qualitative research methodology, covering designing research questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small-team projects; it directly implements the Introduction to Qualitative Methods component of the target

teaches multivariate statistics such as regression, factor analysis, ANOVA and logistic regression for research on human behaviour, and recommends itself for research in political science and sociology; it extends the quantitative training beyond the introductory level as a specific complementary contribution

introduces sociological concepts, theories and methods through Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois and through social problems of race, gender and class; it directly addresses the sociology strand of the target, without a focus on European societies

examines contemporary sociological debates on civil society, solidarity, social trust and the public sphere, with research projects for civil-society organisations; it makes a specific contribution to the sociological analysis of collective action and civil society, building on Introduction to Sociology

teaches negotiation theory and practice, including BATNA, ZOPA and interest-based negotiation, through simulations and role-plays; it directly implements the Negotiation Skills component and the negotiation-and-diplomacy interest of the target

develops basic spoken and written communication in Dutch for everyday situations and introduces Dutch culture; it directly implements the second-language skill of the target at beginner level in a single language

explores theories of moral reasoning (virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism) and applies them to practical issues such as equality, war, punishment and future generations; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the normative-ideas strand, without a European focus

covers the drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change, its societal impacts including migration patterns, adaptation and mitigation solutions, and climate governance and justice; it directly implements the climate strand of the concept

introduces sustainability through the planetary-boundaries framework and the concept of a safe operating space for humanity; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the conceptual foundation for the sustainability courses and the gateway to Sustainability Essentials II

builds on Sustainability Essentials I with waves, chemistry and materials science in relation to sustainability and ends in a project that analyses greenwashing; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the required prerequisite for Renewable System Design and as training in assessing sustainability claims

teaches the assessment of energy-use patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or moving to cleaner energy, covering solar, wind and bioenergy with technical and economic analysis and a report for a partner company; it makes a specific complementary contribution by examining the energy-transition options that climate policy seeks to promote

examines sustainability through the lens of governance, asking how sustainability policies are made and enforced at local, national and international level, which actors represent which interests and how public opinion and politics interact; it directly implements the governance strand of climate policy in the concept
Applies persuasion, framing and ethical communication to local sustainability projects, including field reflection and research on communication choices.

compares the risks of climate-change-driven events, teaches geoscience principles and analytical tools, and teaches actions to reduce risk from events such as droughts; it makes a specific complementary contribution on climate adaptation and risk

focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice, using cases from the Environmental Justice Atlas and perspectives such as feminism, anti-colonialism and degrowth; it makes a specific contribution to the societal and justice dimension of climate policy

examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested through texts, films, protest art, slogans and social media, and teaches students to dissect arguments; it makes a specific contribution to the public debate in which climate policy is contested

teaches life-cycle assessment of the environmental impact of products, processes and services and circular-economy strategy through analysis and guest experts; it makes a specific complementary contribution through assessment tools used in sustainability policy, and it is not a course on European law or politics

alternatives.label: European Politics, Law and Society
alternatives.labelReason: EU politics and law combine with history, economics, sociology, political philosophy and social research methods.
alternatives.concept: Study how European institutions and societies developed and how they respond to political and economic change. Combine EU law and politics with history, economics, sociology and research methods.
progression: Law, Society & Justice precedes dependent courses. Introductory economics precedes macroeconomics, and Research Methods & Statistics precedes advanced statistical work.

alternatives.label: European Climate and Sustainability Policy
alternatives.labelReason: Climate science and sustainability practice provide evidence for studying European policy, law, governance and public communication.
alternatives.concept: Study how European institutions and communities respond to climate change. Combine environmental science, economics and European law with sustainability governance, environmental justice and public communication.
alternatives.distinctness: This option adds climate science, life-cycle analysis, renewable-system design, environmental risk and justice, and climate communication. It shares EU institutions, law and economic foundations with the closest option.
traceOverrides: introduces the EU legal order, with examples such as EU rules on reducing plastic bags that have found their way into national laws; in this programme it makes a specific contribution to how European environmental and climate rules are made binding across member states, although it is not a course on climate law

covers the sources of international law, treaties, the use of force, refugee law and environmental law with attention to climate change; in this programme it directly supports the international legal framework within which climate action is taken

introduces the actors, institutions and decision-making rules of the EU and its responses to crises; in this programme it supplies the institutional arena in which European climate policy is decided, as a specific complementary contribution

applies international relations theory to contemporary issues such as climate change and energy, with a UN Security Council negotiation simulation; in this programme it directly addresses the international politics of climate change

provides tools to compare political systems and democracies, including populism, the decline of parties and globalization's effect on domestic politics; in this programme it supplies the comparative analysis of the democratic systems in which climate policy is contested, as a specific complementary contribution

examines authority, freedom, equality, democracy, pluralism, poverty and environmental issues through political-philosophy texts; in this programme its treatment of environmental issues supplies the political-philosophical framing of environmental responsibility and justice, as a specific complementary contribution

investigates the role of government in the economy, including market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation and political economy; in this programme it provides the economic framework for analysing policy instruments that address environmental problems such as climate change, as a specific complementary contribution
progression: Sustainability foundations precede advanced sustainability study. Introductory law and economics precede dependent courses. Climate communication and applied persuasion contribute complementary forms of inquiry.

candidates.label: Europe's diversity, borders, belonging and migration
candidates.reason: Modern History and sociology address migration, nationalism and belonging. Human Rights and EU Law add legal dimensions of rights and movement. Media & Race and histories of empire offer substantive perspectives on exclusion, often outside Europe. These are valuable supports, but a third plan would rely on the same Europe-focused core without a sustained sequence on European migration, borders and belonging.

selection.assessment: Two distinct options address European institutions and social change, and European climate and sustainability policy. Migration, borders and belonging receive relevant historical, sociological and legal coverage, but the available courses do not sustain a separate Europe-focused programme in this direction.

blocks: European history, identity and historical research
Both study modern political orders and changes in sovereignty and national identity. UCR takes a global view from 1815 onward, while Maastricht centres Europe and starts with the French Revolution.

Both train students to work critically with historical sources in research. Back to the Sources is a shorter skills component, while the History Research Seminar runs the full research cycle from research question to a substantial research paper.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Imagining Europe studies the development of European identities; UCR has no course on European identity or culture, and Modern History, which touches national self-determination, is placed with Ruling Europe.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Lifting the Iron Curtain is a regional course on Central and Eastern Europe after communism; no scheduled UCR course addresses that region, and Modern History is placed with Ruling Europe.
EU politics, international relations and negotiation

Both study the actors, institutions and decision-making rules of the EU and the approaches used to study EU politics. Constructing Europe also develops theory and challenges of integration across a full course, while European Union Politics is a single course.
Both introduce the main theories of international relations and apply them to contemporary issues and actors. Theory of International Relations has a global rather than European focus.

Both teach negotiation as a practised skill through simulation and role-play. Negotiation Skills is tied to European and international settings, while Negotiation & Strategic Thinking teaches negotiation in general.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: European Diplomacy in the 21st Century studies EU external action and diplomatic practice; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart, and Theory of International Relations is placed with Globalizing World.

Both introduce the legal order of the EU and its institutions. Ordering Europe is a full course on the autonomous EU legal order and is followed by EU Law II, whereas UCR offers a single foundations course.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: EU Law II is a second EU-law course; UCR offers a single EU-law course, which is placed with Ordering Europe.
UCR supplies macroeconomic tools for analysing policy, growth and international interdependence. Maastricht applies international economics to European integration.

Both address the relationship between market and state in economic policy. Public Economics analyses market failure, public goods, taxation and political economy in general terms, while Governing the European Economy applies the question to the EU.
Research methods, research skills and thesis
Both introduce quantitative research methods, including research design, surveys and descriptive and inferential statistics.
Both introduce qualitative research methods, including formulating questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small research projects.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Working with Research Problems is a programme-specific skills module on handling research problems in European Studies; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart beyond the methods courses placed elsewhere.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: The Academic Workshop I is a seven-EC skills workshop specific to the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Exploring Contemporary Challenges is the first part of the three-part Academic Workshop II in the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Discussing Contemporary Challenges is the second part of the three-part Academic Workshop II in the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Publishing about Contemporary Challenges is the seven-EC final part of Academic Workshop II in the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Research Methods: Interviewing is a four-EC skills module on interview research for thesis students; no scheduled UCR course teaches interviewing, and Qualitative Research Methodology is placed with Introduction to Qualitative Methods.
This Maastricht route requires a 17 EC thesis and a separate 4 EC methods course. UCR displays optional independent research alongside the thesis.
Academic skills, language and open study space

Both develop core academic skills: Personal & Professional Development teaches students to select and critically analyse sources, formulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments, and improve writing and speaking, which is an important part of the function of Research and Writing in European Studies; the UCR course is broader and not specific to European Studies.
Both are language-learning courses. Students of European Studies choose a second language at the Language Centre, and Dutch is a beginner language course at UCR.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the one-EC Student Support Programme is a year-long support module within the European Studies skills trajectory; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart.
The 24 EC elective semester can include a minor, exchange, an internship or approved electives.

notes.text: Maastricht offers dedicated courses on European identity, economic integration, diplomacy and Central and Eastern Europe, alongside a sequence of research workshops. UCR combines EU law and politics with broader disciplinary courses.

The UCR options emphasise either European institutions and society or European climate policy. Maastricht’s final semester includes either a thesis with a separate methods course or a larger Final Project.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht studies Europe through history, politics, international relations, law, economics, philosophy and sociology. Students develop research skills and complete a thesis or Final Project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option connects European institutions and law with history, economics and society. The second applies law and policy to climate and sustainability. Maastricht offers more dedicated European Studies coursework and a required final research component.

curriculum.limitation: This example uses the first-listed options in the restricted choice groups. The 24 EC elective semester remains open.

componentNotes.y2-07: Choose one of EU Law II, External Relations of the EU, or Challenges in Contemporary Democracies.
componentNotes.y2-09: Choose one of four courses. This example uses the first-listed course.
componentNotes.y3-01: Combine approved electives, a minor, study abroad or an internship for 24 EC.
componentNotes.y3-03: Thesis students choose one 4 EC methods course. This example uses Interviewing.
componentNotes.y3-05: Two examiners assess the final work. Students may instead take the 21 EC Final Project, which has limited places and replaces the thesis and methods course.
